findings.title: Regular `bool` variable declarations are silently registered as TYPE_INT, not TYPE_BOOL
findings.description: parse_type_mark(identifier_name, context) is the function that records a declared identifier's data type. In its T_BOOL_TYPE branch, when called for a plain variable declaration (context==2, used by `variable x : bool;` at parser.cpp:1282 and parser.cpp:1471), it calls update_identifier_data_type(identifier_name, TYPE_INT, ...) instead of TYPE_BOOL (contrast with the correctly-coded context==1 branch at line 897 which uses TYPE_BOOL, and the sibling overload for procedure parameters at parser.cpp:1069 which also correctly uses TYPE_BOOL). Every locally/globally declared bool variable (not a parameter, not a procedure return type) therefore carries identifier_data_type==TYPE_INT for the rest of typechecking, corrupting Typechecker::token_types_compatible_at_all's whole type matrix for that variable. Concretely reproduced: `variable flag: bool; variable f: float; r := flag + f;` compiles with zero errors (should be rejected -- arithmetic operators are only defined on int/float per spec item 10, and bool must not silently act as int in +); and `variable flag: bool; variable n: integer; r := flag + n;` also silently accepted. This also interacts with check_return_statement's UB (see other finding): returning a correctly bool-typed local variable from a bool-returning procedure crashes the compiler because the local var looks like TYPE_INT.

findings.title: check_if_statement / check_loop_statement(-equivalent) / check_return_statement are fed the wrong token — the innermost factor's raw token, not the synthesized type of the whole condition/return expression — causing false type errors on valid relational expressions
findings.description: parser::parse_if_statement, parse_loop_statement and parse_return_statement all set `updated_token = expression_parse.resolved_token;` and pass that token straight to check_if_statement / check_return_statement. But token_and_status.resolved_token is threaded up through parse_expression -> parse_arithOp -> parse_relation -> parse_term -> parse_factor purely via `X_parse.resolved_token = Y_parse.resolved_token;` chaining (e.g. parser.cpp:2279 `relation_parse.resolved_token = term_parse.resolved_token;`), which always ends up being the last-parsed *factor* (i.e. the rightmost operand token), never the type actually synthesized by Typechecker::is_valid_operation() for the relation as a whole. As a result, `if (a > b) then` where a and b are floats reports a spurious 'If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer' error (because the token passed to check_if_statement is the raw float identifier b, not the boolean result of a>b). Same mechanism reproduced for loop conditions (`for (i:=0; i<limit)` with limit:float wrongly reports the if-statement wording) and return statements (`return a > b;` from a bool-returning procedure with a,b:float wrongly reports 'Procedure is of type "Float" which is not compatible with return type of "Bool"').

findings.title: Parenthesized sub-expressions never propagate a synthesized type — the raw leftover operand token is reused instead, causing false accept/reject in chained comparisons
findings.description: parser::parse_factor's `(` branch (T_LPARAM) calls parse_expression() for the inner sub-expression but never assigns factor_parse.resolved_token from it (the developer's own comment marks this gap: 'what to do here? COME BACK ... maybe have parse_expression return a token of the type it resolves to?'). Meanwhile Typechecker::feed_in_tokens's post-operation cleanup (`clear_tokens(true)` at Typechecker.cpp:134, implemented at Typechecker.cpp:245-260) discards the synthesized result and instead promotes the raw second_token (the last literal operand fed) into first_token for whatever comes next. So after computing `(a > b)`, the typechecker's internal 'current type' for subsequent chaining is literally b's own declared type (e.g. float), not the boolean result of the comparison. This produces false rejections: `(a > b) > p` where a:integer, b:float, p:bool (a legal type-correct expression: bool compared with bool) is rejected with 'Type "Float" and type "Bool" have no valid operations' -- the checker is actually comparing b(float) against p(bool), not the real bool result of (a>b) against p.

findings.title: Unary prefix operators ('not' and unary '-') desync feed_in_tokens's accumulator, silently disabling type checking for the entire remaining expression
findings.description: feed_in_tokens's very first branch unconditionally assigns whatever token arrives first to first_token: `if (first_token.type == T_NULL) { first_token = token_to_feed; ... }`. Both T_NOT ('not', fed at parser.cpp:2021 for a leading `not <arithOp>`) and T_MINUS (fed at the start of parse_arithOp for `<arithOp> - <relation>` and at parse_factor for unary `[-] <name>`) are classified as 'relationship' tokens by token_is_relationship (Typechecker.cpp:172-174, 180-182), but because they are typically the very first token fed for the statement, this first-branch check fires before token_is_relationship is ever consulted, so the unary operator token itself becomes first_token (as if it were an operand) instead of being pushed onto relation_tokens. The real first operand then lands in second_token, relation_tokens stays empty, are_tokens_full() (which requires relation_tokens.size()>0) never becomes true, and every subsequent token for that statement falls into feed_in_tokens's terminal `else { /* too many tokens */ }` branch (Typechecker.cpp:120-123) and is silently dropped. Net effect: any expression beginning with `not` or unary `-` bypasses type checking entirely for the rest of that expression/statement.

findings.title: Bitwise/logical '&' and '|' have no case in is_valid_operation's operator switch, so they bypass all type validation and produce no diagnostics
findings.description: Spec item 10 states bitwise & and | are 'valid only on variables of type integer', with separate logical &, |, and not semantics for booleans. token_is_relationship (Typechecker.cpp:148-150, 192-194) marks T_AMPERSAND and T_VERTICAL_BAR as relation-class tokens, and the parser feeds them into feed_in_tokens exactly like any other binary operator (parser.cpp:2005/2013/2039/2044). But Typechecker::is_valid_operation's switch over relation_tokens[0].type (Typechecker.cpp:308-473, one-relation-token case) only has cases for T_PLUS, T_MINUS, T_GREATER, T_LESS, T_MULT, T_SLASH; T_AMPERSAND and T_VERTICAL_BAR fall into `default: return_value = false; return_object.valid_parse = return_value; return return_object;` (Typechecker.cpp:469-472) with no call to generate_error_report and no synthesized resolved_token. Since the parser also never checks feed_in_tokens's return value at these call sites, this means & and | are never actually type-checked at all: illegal uses (e.g. float & float, which spec explicitly disallows) are silently accepted with zero diagnostics, exactly the same as legal uses (int & int).
findings.evidence:
Typechecker.cpp:469-472 (default case of the size==1 switch, no error report call), contrasted with every other case (e.g. T_PLUS at 311-338) which calls parser_parent->generate_error_report(...) on failure.
Runtime proof: a,b,c all declared `float`; `c := a & b;` -> 'The program parsed successfully with no errors' (spec item 10: '& ... valid only on variables of type integer').

findings.title: Typechecker has no notion of arrays at all: is_array is never consulted, and array-index-must-be-integer is an unimplemented TODO
findings.description: token::is_array (token.h:128) is set by the parser when it sees bracket syntax (parser.cpp:1957, parser.cpp:2510) but is never read anywhere in Typechecker.cpp (confirmed via grep across the file). token_types_compatible_at_all/is_valid_operation only ever compare base data_types (int/float/bool/string) between first_token and second_token, so an array reference and a scalar of the same base type are indistinguishable to the typechecker, contrary to spec item 9 ('Assignment of array variables ... permitted provided the source and destination array types are of the same length'). Separately, spec item 13 ('Array indexes must be of type integer') is left as an explicit unimplemented TODO by the original author right where the index expression is parsed.

findings.title: second_relation_token_chains falls off the end of a non-void function (UB, g++ emits ud2 -> SIGILL) for every chained two-character relational operator except leading '&'/'|'/'-'/'*'/not/'+'/'/'
findings.description: second_relation_token_chains only returns explicitly when the second incoming token is not T_ASSIGN (returns false) or when previous_token_type falls into the switch's `default:` (also returns false); for the else-branch switch on relation_tokens[0].type, cases T_ASSIGN, T_COLON, T_EXCLAM, T_GREATER, T_LESS all just `break;` with no return, so control falls off the end of the function -- undefined behavior. g++ -Wreturn-type confirms this ('control reaches end of non-void function' at line 243). This is reached whenever the second token of a relation is '=' and the first relation token was '=', '!', '>', or '<' -- i.e. every occurrence of '==', '!=', '>=', '<=' in the source (T_COLON as relation_tokens[0] appears practically unreachable, since ':' is never fed into the typechecker during assignment parsing -- those feed_in_tokens calls are commented out at parser.cpp:1593/1605). Compiled and run: testPgms/correct/math.src and testPgms/correct/logicals.src (both use '==') crash the built compiler with exit code 132 (SIGILL).
findings.evidence: g++ -c Typechecker.cpp -g -Wall -Wextra: 'Typechecker.cpp:243:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function [-Wreturn-type]'. Typechecker.cpp:216-239 switch has no return in any case, only `break;`. Runtime: `./compiler testPgms/correct/math.src` -> exit 132; `./compiler testPgms/correct/logicals.src` -> exit 132.

findings.title: check_return_statement falls off the end of a non-void function (UB/SIGILL) for every spec-legal implicit-conversion return (int<->float, int<->bool) -- only exact type matches survive
findings.description: check_return_statement explicitly returns false when incompatible, and explicitly returns true only in the `if (token_one_type == token_two_type)` sub-case; when compatible==true but token_one_type != token_two_type (e.g. int returned where the procedure is declared float, or vice versa, or bool<->int) there is no return statement, so control falls off the end -- UB, confirmed by g++ -Wreturn-type. Because the type matrix (token_types_compatible_at_all) marks int/float and int/bool pairs as 'compatible' but not equal, essentially every spec-legal implicit-conversion return (spec item 14: 'bool and integer types are compatible, and integer and float types are compatible') crashes the compiler; only an exact-type-match return works. This interacts with the TYPE_INT-mis-registration bug (separate finding): returning a *correctly bool-typed* local variable from a bool-returning procedure also crashes, because the local variable's identifier_data_type was silently corrupted to TYPE_INT at declaration time, making it look like an int-vs-bool mismatch to check_return_statement.

findings.title: check_assignment_statement is a stub that always returns true; LHS/RHS assignment compatibility (spec item 14) is never enforced
findings.description: check_assignment_statement ignores both parameters and unconditionally returns true, so no assignment in the whole language is ever type-checked (target and expression types are never compared, contrary to spec item 14). Confirmed independently via a fresh read and a runtime test.

findings.title: check_loop_statement is dead code; parse_loop_statement calls check_if_statement instead, giving loop-condition errors misleading 'If statements' wording
findings.description: check_loop_statement (Typechecker.cpp:1297-1315, with its own distinct error text 'Loop statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer') is never called anywhere (grep across parser.cpp/Typechecker.cpp/Typechecker.h/main.cpp finds zero call sites). parse_loop_statement instead calls type_checker->check_if_statement(updated_token) at parser.cpp:1808, so any loop-condition type error is reported with the wrong ('If statements ...') message. Independently confirmed by grep and by the runtime test above ('for (i:=0; i<limit)' with limit:float reports 'If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer').

findings.title: token::identifier_data_type has no default member initializer, unlike its sibling fields
findings.description: Every other data member of `token` (type, line_found, scope_id, intValue, stringValue, boolValue, floatValue, charValue, first_token_on_line, identifer_type, is_array) has an explicit default value, but `data_types identifier_data_type;` does not, so a default-constructed token carries an indeterminate value in this field. Typechecker::token_types_compatible_at_all switches on first_token.identifier_data_type / second_token.identifier_data_type whenever a token is classified as T_IDENTIFIER; any code path that feeds an identifier-typed token into the typechecker without having first resolved it through a scope lookup (update_context_token) would read this indeterminate value, and the switch's `default:` fallthrough leaves the corresponding typechecker_types field at its typechecker_null default, later reaching give_token_type_name (see separate finding) with no matching case. I could not construct a concrete reproduction from the current parser call sites (which do appear to always resolve identifiers via update_context_token before feeding them), so this is flagged as a latent robustness risk rather than a confirmed live bug.
findings.evidence: token.h:107-128 shows explicit defaults for every field except line 126: `data_types identifier_data_type;` with no `= TYPE_NONE`.

findings.title: give_token_type_name has no case (and no default) for typechecker_null, producing an empty type name in error messages
findings.description: give_token_type_name's switch handles typechecker_bool/float/int/string but not typechecker_null and has no default case (confirmed by g++ -Wswitch: 'enumeration value typechecker_null not handled in switch'). token_types_and_status::token_one_type/token_two_type default-initialize to typechecker_null (Typechecker.h:36-37) and several branches of token_types_compatible_at_all's nested switches (e.g. the `default:` cases for unmapped identifier_data_type, Typechecker.cpp:747-750, 857-860, 967-970, 1077-1080) leave one side unset. If reached, is_valid_operation's error message would read as e.g. 'Type "" and type "Bool" have no valid operations' with a blank type name instead of a real diagnostic, obscuring the actual cause. Not independently confirmed with a runtime reproduction.
findings.evidence: g++ -Wall -Wextra: 'Typechecker.cpp: In member function std::string Typechecker::give_token_type_name(typechecker_types): Typechecker.cpp:1151:12: warning: enumeration value typechecker_null not handled in switch [-Wswitch]'. Typechecker.cpp:1148-1170 has no default: clause.

findings.title: parse_relation's leading '!=' branch never feeds the typechecker nor parses a term, leaving term_parse unassigned in that branch
findings.description: In parse_relation, the branches for a *leading* T_LESS/T_GREATER/T_ASSIGN all call type_checker->feed_in_tokens(...) and then parse_term() for the right-hand operand. The T_EXCLAM branch (a leading '!=' at the start of what should be a <relation>, which per the grammar should never legitimately happen since <relation> always starts with <term>) does neither: it only advances past '!' and checks for a following '=', producing an error if there isn't one, but never calls feed_in_tokens or parse_term(). If this branch is taken, `relation_parse.resolved_token = term_parse.resolved_token;` at line 2279 reads a term_parse local that was never assigned in this branch (though token_and_status has in-class default member initializers, so this is not raw garbage, just semantically meaningless). I tested a minimal malformed-input case (`if (!= 5) then`) and it did not crash the compiler (parser error-recovery intervened before this path mattered visibly), so I cannot confirm a user-visible defect beyond the dead/incomplete code itself.

findings.title: Several Typechecker methods (second_to_first, is_valid_relation, statement_is_finished) are unused stubs that always return true
findings.description: is_valid_relation() (Typechecker.cpp:16-20) and statement_is_finished() (Typechecker.cpp:22-26) unconditionally return true and are never called anywhere in parser.cpp or Typechecker.cpp. second_to_first() (Typechecker.cpp:28-35) is likewise never called (its only reference anywhere is a commented-out call at parser.cpp:2352). These are inert scaffolding left over from an earlier design and represent dead surface area rather than active bugs.
findings.evidence: grep -n "second_to_first\|is_valid_relation()\|statement_is_finished()" parser.cpp Typechecker.cpp shows only the definitions plus one commented-out call site (parser.cpp:2352: `//type_checker->second_to_first();`).

notes:
Scope covered: Typechecker.cpp/.h in full, plus the parser.cpp call sites that feed tokens into the typechecker (feed_in_tokens call sites across parse_expression/parse_arithOp/parse_relation/parse_term/parse_factor/parse_name), declaration handling that populates identifier_data_type (parse_type_mark overloads), and if/loop/return statement handling. Built the project with `make` (plain g++ -g, no optimization) and ran ~15 small (3-13 line) .src test programs through ./compiler to empirically confirm behavior rather than relying on static reading alone; all test files were written to the scratch directory only (no repo files were modified). Cross-checked every claim against spec2023.txt semantics section (items 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) before flagging as a spec violation.

Known-list overlap handled per instructions: check_assignment_statement (stub), check_loop_statement (dead code, replaced by check_if_statement), and second_relation_token_chains/check_return_statement (missing-return UB/SIGILL) are all mentioned in the repo's CLAUDE.md 'Known broken state' section. I independently re-derived and runtime-confirmed each of these rather than parroting the doc, and where possible added new precision beyond what CLAUDE.md states (e.g. the exact operator-sequence trigger set for second_relation_token_chains; the exact compatible-but-unequal-type trigger condition for check_return_statement's crash, including its novel interaction with the TYPE_INT mis-registration bug). The remaining findings (bool-declared-as-int mis-registration; wrong-token bugs in check_if_statement/check_return_statement/loop; parenthesized-subexpression type loss; unary-prefix state-machine desync for 'not'/'-'; missing & / | validation; and the complete absence of array-aware type checking) are, to the best of my determination from a fresh reading, not documented anywhere in the repo and are all backed by concrete runtime reproductions using minimal (3-13 line) programs, which are the requested 'concrete example programs' for each defect.

Test scratch files used for reproduction are under /tmp/claude-1000/-datadrive-data-compiler-course/e0905122-5395-4b36-add9-f6a81e41bd28/scratchpad/tests/ (and.src source, no repo files touched): and_test.src, and_bad_test.src, and_float_test.src, not_test.src, not_bad_test.src, not_control_test2.src, bool_decl_test.src, bool_plus_int.src, string_plus_int.src, return_crash_test.src, bool_return_test.src, paren_misfire_test2.src, if_wrong_token_test.src, return_wrong_token_test.src, loop_wrong_token_test.src, unary_minus_bypass_test.src, assign_stub_test.src, leading_exclam_test.src.
